title: Our Environment
subject: science
syllabus_note: Follows the CBSE 2025-26 syllabus: eco-system, environmental problems, ozone depletion, waste production and their solutions; biodegradable and non-biodegradable substances.

blocks.title: Where does your garbage go?
blocks.body:
Every day each home throws away vegetable peels, plastic wrappers, paper and broken things. Some of it disappears into the soil within weeks; some of it will still be lying around when you are a grandparent.

In this chapter you will see how living and non-living things work together in an **ecosystem**, how energy flows through food chains, how harmful chemicals collect in our bodies, why the ozone layer matters, and how each of us can manage waste better.

blocks.title: The man who cleaned a beach
blocks.body:
In 2015, Afroz Shah, a young lawyer in Mumbai, was upset to see Versova beach buried under knee-deep plastic. With one elderly neighbour he began picking up rubbish every weekend.

Thousands of volunteers joined him, and over the next years they removed millions of kilograms of waste; turtles came back to nest on the beach. In 2016 the United Nations named him a **Champion of the Earth**.
blocks.future: Environmental science leads to careers in ecology, waste management, pollution control, climate science, environmental law and sustainable design.

blocks.question: If all the frogs in a field disappeared, what would happen to the number of insects?
blocks.explanation: Frogs eat insects; without them, the insects would multiply. Removing one link disturbs the whole food chain.

blocks.title: Biotic and abiotic components
blocks.body:
An **ecosystem** is made up of all the living organisms in an area together with the non-living components, interacting with one another.

- **Biotic components:** the living things: plants, animals and microorganisms.
- **Abiotic components:** the non-living things: temperature, rainfall, wind, soil and minerals.

Forests, ponds and lakes are **natural ecosystems**; gardens, crop fields and aquariums are **artificial (human-made) ecosystems**.

By the way they get food, organisms are:
- **Producers:** green plants and blue-green algae, which make food by photosynthesis.
- **Consumers:** herbivores, carnivores, omnivores and parasites, which eat food made by producers directly or indirectly.
- **Decomposers:** bacteria and fungi, which break down dead remains and waste into simple substances that go back into the soil and are used again by plants.

blocks.question: Which of these is an artificial ecosystem?
blocks.explanation: An aquarium is made and maintained by humans; forests, lakes and ponds are natural.

sections.title: Food chains and the flow of energy

blocks.title: Trophic levels and the 10% law
blocks.body:
A **food chain** is a series of organisms in which each one eats the one before it: grass → deer → lion. Each step is a **trophic level**.

**Energy flow:**
- Green plants capture only about **1%** of the sunlight falling on their leaves.
- At each step, a large part of the food energy is used by the organism for its own life processes and lost as heat; only about **10%** is passed on to the next level (the **10 per cent law**).
- So food chains usually have only **three or four** steps; there is too little energy left for more. The number of organisms is also usually largest at the producer level.
- Energy flow is **unidirectional**: energy captured by producers does not go back to the Sun, and energy passed to herbivores does not come back to plants.

In nature, food chains are interconnected: one organism is eaten by several others, forming a **food web**.

blocks.title: Trophic levels in a food chain
blocks.body:
| Trophic level | Who | Example (grass → grasshopper → frog → snake → eagle) |
|---|---|---|
| First | producers (autotrophs) | grass |
| Second | primary consumers (herbivores) | grasshopper |
| Third | secondary consumers (small carnivores) | frog |
| Fourth | tertiary consumers (large carnivores) | snake |
| Fifth | top carnivore | eagle |

blocks.question: If 10 000 J of energy is available at the producer level, how much reaches the tertiary consumers?

blocks.title: Poisons that pile up
blocks.body:
Many **pesticides and chemicals** are used to protect crops. Some of them are washed into the soil and water, absorbed by plants and taken up by animals.

Such chemicals are **not degradable**, so they are not broken down in the body and they accumulate. Each organism eats many organisms from the level below, so the concentration **increases at each trophic level**. This is **biological magnification**. Since humans are at the top of many food chains, the maximum concentration of these chemicals collects in our bodies.

This is why food grains, vegetables and fruits, and even ready-made foods, can contain pesticide residues; washing food and reducing pesticide use help.

blocks.question: In the food chain grass → grasshopper → frog → snake → eagle, which organism will have the highest concentration of a non-degradable pesticide?
blocks.explanation: The concentration increases at every level, so the top consumer, the eagle, has the most.
option_feedback: It is low in the chain.
Snakes and eagles above it collect more.

blocks.title: Earth's sunscreen
blocks.body:
**Ozone (O₃)** is a molecule made of three oxygen atoms. At ground level it is a deadly poison, but high in the atmosphere it forms a layer that **shields the earth from harmful ultraviolet (UV) radiation** of the Sun. UV radiation can cause skin cancer and damages living things.

**How ozone forms:** high-energy UV radiation splits some oxygen molecules into free oxygen atoms: $\mathrm{O_{2} \rightarrow O + O}$ The oxygen atoms then combine with oxygen molecules to form ozone: $\mathrm{O + O_{2} \rightarrow O_{3}}$

**Ozone depletion:** the amount of ozone began to drop sharply in the 1980s. This was linked to synthetic chemicals such as **chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs)**, used as refrigerants and in fire extinguishers. In 1987 the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) succeeded in forging an agreement to freeze CFC production at 1986 levels. It is now mandatory for manufacturing companies worldwide to make CFC-free refrigerators.

blocks.question: The ozone layer protects us by:
options: keeping the earth warm at night
absorbing harmful UV radiation from the Sun
blocks.explanation: The ozone layer absorbs most of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet radiation.
option_feedback: That is not the role of ozone.

blocks.title: Biodegradable and non-biodegradable
blocks.body:
Substances that are broken down by biological processes (by bacteria and other decomposers) are **biodegradable**; those that are not are **non-biodegradable**. Enzymes are specific: they break down only certain substances, so plastics and many synthetic chemicals are not digested by microbes.

| Biodegradable | Non-biodegradable |
|---|---|
| broken down by bacteria and other decomposers | not broken down by biological processes |
| vegetable peels, paper, cotton, wood, leaves, cow dung | plastic, polythene, glass, metals, DDT, many synthetic chemicals |
| return nutrients to the soil, but harm the environment if in large amounts | stay for a very long time, pile up, and harm soil, water and living things |

**Changes in packaging:** once, food came wrapped in leaves or paper, and tea was served in clay cups (kulhads). Now plastic packaging and disposable cups create mountains of waste. (Using kulhads on a huge scale also has a cost: it uses up the fertile topsoil.)

**What each of us can do:** separate wet (biodegradable) and dry waste; compost kitchen waste; carry cloth bags; avoid single-use plastic; **reduce, reuse and recycle**; dispose of electronic items carefully, because they contain hazardous materials.

blocks.question: Which of these groups contains only biodegradable items?
blocks.explanation: Cake, wood and grass are all broken down by decomposers; plastic, glass and polythene are not.

blocks.title: Ten per cent and three R's
blocks.body:
- **10% law:** "Each step keeps 90, passes 10." 10 000 → 1000 → 100 → 10.
- **Magnification goes up, energy goes down** the food chain.
- **Ozone:** O₂ splits (UV), O joins O₂ → O₃; CFCs destroy it.
- **Waste:** Reduce → Reuse → Recycle, in that order of priority.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.body:
- Saying that energy flows in a cycle: energy flow is one-way; it is nutrients that cycle.
- Saying that the top consumer has the least pesticide: it has the **most** (biological magnification), even though it gets the least energy.
- Calling ozone harmless everywhere: at ground level it is a poison.
- Assuming that biodegradable waste has no effect: in large amounts it produces foul smell, disease and greenhouse gases.
- Writing that decomposers are consumers that eat living things: they break down dead remains.

blocks.title: Try it in class
blocks.body: Bury a vegetable peel, a paper scrap, a piece of plastic and a piece of glass in pots of moist soil; dig them up after a month and compare. Play a food-chain game with energy tokens: start with 1000 beads at the producer, and pass only one bead in ten to each next player to show why chains are short.

blocks.title: Explain it in your own words
blocks.body: Explain to a friend why an eagle has more pesticide in its body than a grasshopper, even though it eats far less grass.

blocks.title: Where this leads
blocks.body:
- **Chapter 5, Life Processes:** autotrophs and heterotrophs are the producers and consumers of ecosystems.
- **Chapter 4:** CFCs and polythene are carbon compounds that do not break down easily.
- **Class 12 Biology:** ecosystems, biodiversity and environmental issues in detail.

blocks.title: Mastery challenge
blocks.body:
In a pond, the food chain is: algae → water insects → small fish → large fish → fish-eating bird. The algae trap 50 000 J of energy.

(a) How much energy reaches the large fish? (b) Which organism will have the highest concentration of a pesticide that entered the pond? (c) What would happen if all the small fish were removed?

**Answer:** (a) 10% at each step: 50 000 → 5000 (insects) → 500 (small fish) → **50 J** (large fish). (b) The fish-eating bird, at the top. (c) The water insects would increase (no predators), and the large fish and birds would decline for lack of food; the balance of the pond would be disturbed.

blocks.title: Chapter summary
blocks.body:
- An ecosystem has biotic (living) and abiotic (non-living) components; it can be natural (forest, pond) or artificial (garden, aquarium).
- Producers, consumers and decomposers form food chains and food webs; each step is a trophic level.
- Energy flow is one-way and only about 10% passes to the next level, so food chains are short.
- Non-degradable chemicals increase in concentration at each level: biological magnification.
- The ozone layer absorbs harmful UV radiation; CFCs deplete it, and their production has been controlled.
- Biodegradable and non-biodegradable wastes must be separated and managed: reduce, reuse, recycle.

blocks.title: Board exam tips
blocks.body:
- Always write food chains with arrows from food to eater (grass → deer → lion).
- Use the 10% law step by step in energy questions.
- Learn the ozone equations and the role of CFCs and UNEP (1987).
- In 'give two ways' questions about waste, give specific actions (cloth bags, composting, separating wet and dry waste).

blocks.front: What is the 10 per cent law?
blocks.back: Only about 10% of the energy at one trophic level is passed on to the next.
The increase in concentration of non-degradable chemicals at each successive trophic level.
